description.summary: Malevolent supernatural entities found across world religions and cultures. Demons are typically depicted as evil spirits, fallen angels, or spiritual beings that oppose good, tempt humans, cause harm, and may possess individuals. The concept varies significantly between religious traditions.
description.full: Demons are malevolent supernatural entities present in virtually every major religious and cultural tradition worldwide. In Abrahamic religions (Christianity, Islam, Judaism), demons are often understood as fallen angels who rebelled against God or evil spirits that tempt and harm humanity. In Eastern religions, similar entities exist with varying characteristics—Hindu Rakshasas, Buddhist Maras, Japanese Oni. Demonology encompasses the systematic study of demons, their hierarchies, and classifications. Historical demon beliefs have been invoked to explain mental illness, misfortune, disease, and moral failings. Possession by demons has been reported across cultures, leading to exorcism practices. While demons are primarily theological concepts, belief in demonic entities remains strong in many religious communities, and reported experiences of demonic encounters continue to this day. The study of demons intersects theology, psychology, anthropology, and folklore studies.

etymology.origin: From Ancient Greek 'daimōn' (δαίμων), originally meaning a spirit or divine power without inherently evil connotation. Through Latin 'daemon' and Christian interpretation, the term acquired its negative meaning of evil spirit.

origins.cultural_roots: Belief in malevolent supernatural entities is among humanity's oldest and most universal spiritual concepts. Mesopotamian religions had extensive demon catalogues by 3000 BCE. Zoroastrianism (1500 BCE) established dualistic good-vs-evil framework influencing later religions.
origins.earliest_accounts: Sumerian and Akkadian texts describe demons like Pazuzu (demon of wind and plague), Lamashtu (child-killing demon), and others. Egyptian texts mention demons and evil spirits. Ancient Greek daimones were originally neutral but acquired negative associations.
origins.religious_development: Abrahamic religions developed sophisticated demonologies: Jewish tradition established demons in Talmudic texts; Christianity systematized fallen angel theology; Islam incorporated jinn and shayatin into cosmology.

history.modern_era: Demon belief remains strong in religious communities worldwide. The Catholic Church continues to train exorcists and perform exorcisms. Protestant, Orthodox, Islamic, Hindu, and Buddhist traditions maintain exorcism practices. Psychology and psychiatry have provided alternative explanations for alleged possession (mental illness, dissociative disorders, cultural conditioning). However, religious authorities maintain demons are real spiritual threats. Popular culture continues fascination with demonic themes.

notable.name: Loudun Possessions
notable.description: Ursuline nuns in Loudun convent claimed to be possessed by demons sent by Father Urbain Grandier. The nuns exhibited convulsions, blasphemy, sexual behavior, and speaking in tongues. Public exorcisms were performed. Grandier was convicted of witchcraft and burned at the stake. Modern historians suggest mass hysteria, sexual repression, and political machinations rather than genuine possession.

conditions.context: Religious tensions, convent life, political intrigue

credibility.notes: Real historical event; demonic possession claim disputed by historians

sources: Huxley, A. (1952). The Devils of Loudun

notable.name: Exorcism of Anneliese Michel
notable.description: Anneliese Michel, a German woman, was diagnosed with epilepsy and depression. After medical treatments failed, she and her family sought Catholic exorcism. Over 10 months, 67 exorcism sessions were performed. Anneliese exhibited disturbing behaviors: speaking in multiple voices, self-harm, refusing food. She claimed possession by multiple demons including Lucifer, Judas, Nero, Cain, Hitler, and Fleischmann (a disgraced priest). She died of malnutrition and dehydration. Her parents and the exorcists were convicted of negligent homicide. Medical experts concluded she suffered from epilepsy and psychosis. The case raised profound questions about possession vs. mental illness.

factors: Medical diagnosis of epilepsy and psychosis
credibility.notes: Tragic case illustrating dangers of attributing mental illness to demons

sources: Goodman, F. (2005). The Exorcism of Anneliese Michel
Nicola, U. (2016). Anneliese Michel - A True Story of a Case of Demonic Possession

notable.name: Roland Doe Exorcism (Inspired The Exorcist)
notable.description: A 13-year-old boy (pseudonym Roland Doe or Robbie Mannheim) reportedly exhibited disturbing behaviors after his aunt (a spiritualist) died. Objects moved, scratching sounds, bed shaking, speaking in Latin, violent reactions to religious objects. Catholic priests performed multiple exorcism rituals over several weeks. The case was kept secret for decades but inspired William Peter Blatty's novel The Exorcist. Skeptics note the boy was likely troubled, suggestible, and acting out, possibly with some psychosomatic symptoms.

theological.name: Fallen Angel Doctrine (Christian/Jewish)
theological.description: Demons are angels who rebelled against God alongside Lucifer and were cast out of heaven. They now oppose God's will and corrupt humanity.

theological.name: Jinn Theology (Islamic)
theological.description: Demons are jinn (beings made of smokeless fire) who chose evil. Iblis (Satan) is a jinn who refused to bow to Adam. Not all jinn are demons; they have free will.

theological.name: Primordial Evil
theological.description: Demons are manifestations or agents of cosmic evil, existing in opposition to good. May be personifications of chaos, darkness, or death.

psychological.name: Mental Illness Misattribution
psychological.description: Alleged demon possession is actually mental illness—schizophrenia, dissociative identity disorder, psychosis, epilepsy—misinterpreted through religious lens.

psychological.name: Dissociative Identity Disorder
psychological.description: Multiple personality states misinterpreted as demon possession. Trauma victims may develop alternate identities perceived as demons.

psychological.name: Suggestion and Expectation
psychological.description: Religious expectation and cultural scripts lead people to interpret experiences as demonic. Exorcism rituals reinforce belief.
evidence_cited: Hypnotic suggestion can produce similar effects

sociological.name: Social Scapegoating
sociological.description: Demon beliefs used to explain and control deviant behavior, illness, or misfortune. Serves social function of maintaining norms.
evidence_cited: Possession claims often involve sexual or rebellious behavior

sociological.name: Mass Hysteria
sociological.description: Group possession cases (Loudun, convents) result from mass psychogenic illness—stress, anxiety, and suggestion spreading through groups.

neurological.name: Temporal Lobe Epilepsy
neurological.description: Seizure activity in temporal lobe can produce religious experiences, hearing voices, personality changes misinterpreted as possession.
evidence_cited: Temporal lobe epilepsy symptoms overlap with possession
Brain stimulation can produce religious experiences

neurological.name: Sleep Paralysis and Hypnagogic States
neurological.description: Sleep-related phenomena produce sensation of presence, pressure on chest, inability to move—interpreted as demonic attack.

skeptical.name: Cultural Construct
skeptical.description: Demons are entirely cultural constructs—mythological beings invented to explain misfortune, enforce morality, and express psychological fears. No evidence for objective existence.
evidence_cited: Natural explanations available for all claims
Coincides with religious decline in developed nations

paranormal.name: Non-Human Entities
paranormal.description: Demons are real non-corporeal entities, possibly interdimensional beings, that interact with humans. Not necessarily tied to religious frameworks.

folklore.beliefs: Demons play central roles in moral frameworks—representing temptation, evil, and spiritual danger. Protective practices include prayer, amulets, rituals, and avoiding certain behaviors.

methods: Wearing protective amulets (crosses, hamsa, Quranic verses, protection mantras)

cultural.sensitivity_note: Demon beliefs are deeply held religious convictions for billions of people worldwide. Approach with respect for diverse faith traditions. Avoid mockery or dismissiveness. Many individuals have genuine, frightening experiences they attribute to demons. Whether explained religiously, psychologically, or as cultural phenomena, these experiences are real to those who have them.

research.ongoing_studies: Demon belief and possession continue to be studied by theologians, psychologists, anthropologists, and paranormal researchers. Catholic Church reports increased demand for exorcism in 21st century. Psychology studies dissociative phenomena and cultural expression of distress. Anthropology examines possession rituals across cultures. No scientific consensus supports supernatural demon existence, but religious traditions maintain theological positions.
